digm-553/assignments/asn-2-—-critical-te.title: Critical Technical Journal
digm-553/assignments/asn-2-—-critical-te.description:
Weight: 25%Throughout the course, maintain a journal documenting your making process and reflexive critique. This journal captures all smaller post-class deliverables.
Technical Documentation — What did you make, what did you try, what broke?
Epistemic Interrogation — What is your tool thinking? What does your process assume?
Entanglement Mapping — How are you, your tools, and your materials mutually transforming each other?
Covers course opening through proposal. Includes:
Journal Entry 0: Potluck reflection (Week 2)
Journal Entry 1: Epistemic Tool Audit (Week 3) — choose one software + one hardware tool; map what each knows, assumes, and forecloses
Speculative Proposal (see ASN 1)
Deep making phase. Includes:
Journal Entry 2: First Impasse Report (Week 5) — what has resisted; what the impasse reveals
Mid-term presentation materials
Final development phase. Includes:
Journal Entry 3: Process Seed Reflection (Week 8) — what emerged from the seed exchange
Final project documentation
The journal can take many forms: physical notebook, blog, digital whiteboard, PDF, video diary, etc. Format can be negotiated with the instructor. Installments submitted as PDF to Blackboard at three specific checkpoints.Depth of engagement, documentation quality, honest tracking of failure/pivot.

digm-553/assignments/asn-3-—-experimenta.title: Experimental Media Project
digm-553/assignments/asn-3-—-experimenta.description: Weight: 35%Develop an original digital media project that demonstrates thinking-in-action. Projects are encouraged to utilize physical computing hardware entangled with software environments. Evaluated on the rigor of the path taken, not just final polish.This is not a "make a cool thing" assignment. It is a research-creation project: the making process is the research. The project should demonstrate how your encounter with tools and materials transformed your initial inquiry. The project should show evidence of risk, impasse, pivot, and transformation.Projects should engage with at least one physical computing element (Adafruit QT Py RP2040, MPR121 touch sensor, or equivalent) entangled with a software environment (TouchDesigner, Max/MSP, p5.js, Pure Data, Unity, or equivalent).Early explorations feeding into the Speculative Proposal.Mid-term presentation focuses on what isn't working and what that reveals. Not a polish presentation — an honest reckoning with impasse.Final build + documentation uploaded to Blackboard. Documentation should include: project description, process narrative, technical documentation, and reflection on how the project changed from proposal to completion.Creative risk, conceptual-material integration, technical engagement, research-creation methodology.

digm-553/assignments/asn-5-—-final-prese.title: Final Presentation
digm-553/assignments/asn-5-—-final-prese.description:
Weight: 20%Render your work public. This 12–15 minute presentation (Week 11) should expose the formative forces of the project.This is not "here is what I made." It is: here is how the encounter with tools/materials changed the inquiry. The process is part of the work. The presentation must make the invisible labor, decisions, pivots, and transformations visible.
Entry point — What was your driving curiosity? What was your dog?
The matter-network — What tools/materials were you entangled with?
Impasses and pivots — What resisted? What did that reveal?
The work — Demonstration/documentation of the project
Formative forces — How did the encounter with tools/materials change the inquiry?
Open questions — What does this work open that it doesn't answer?
Recorded presentation with demonstration. 12–15 minutes.Documentation (slides, video, or equivalent) submitted to Blackboard. Revised Speculative Proposal also due this week.

digm-553/assignments/asn-1-—-potluck-+-s.title: Potluck + Speculative Proposal

digm-553/assignments/asn-4-—-structured-.title: Structured Dialogue + Participation
digm-553/assignments/asn-4-—-structured-.description:
Weight: 10%Participation in two formal review sessions (Weeks 6 & 9) and the mid-term presentation (Week 7). This grade also encompasses larger class engagement throughout.Critique sessions utilize the Six Thinking Hats format to focus on activating potential rather than rendering judgment:
White Hat — Facts and data: what is actually here?
Red Hat — Intuition and feeling: what does this project make you feel?
Black Hat — Caution: what are the risks or gaps?
Yellow Hat — Optimism: what is the potential?
Green Hat — Creativity: what else could this become?
Blue Hat — Process: what questions should we be asking?

digm-553/documents/hardware-clarificatio.title: Hardware Clarifications — Thinking Toward Sensors
digm-553/documents/hardware-clarificatio.description:
You may have heard the terms Stemma QT and Qwiic and Grove in lecture and wondered if they're different systems you need to choose between. They aren’t, really. There are some subtle differences between them, besides name, but they are types of either 3 prong or 4 prong connectors.Stemma QT (Adafruit) and Qwiic (SparkFun) are two brand names for the same electrical standard: a 4-pin JST-SH connector running I2C communication at 3.3V. The physical connector is identical. The electrical protocol is (nearly) identical. A Stemma QT cable plugs into a Qwiic board and vice versa, witt little to no modification needed.
Here is a working definition for this course:A sensor is anything that transduces a physical phenomenon into data your system can process.That definition is deliberately broad. It includes: An accelerometer/IMU that reads movement, orientation, and vibration A capacitive touch sensor that reads electrical conductance at discrete points A microphone that reads acoustic pressure over time A webcam that reads light as a 2D pixel grid at some frame rate A Kinect or depth camera that reads spatial distance and skeletal pose A GSR (galvanic skin response) sensor that reads electrodermal conductance as a proxy for physiological arousal A piezoelectric disc that reads mechanical deformation (pressure, impact, vibration) A GPS module that reads position in space relative to satellites A light sensor or color sensor that reads photon flux at various wavelengths A flex sensor that reads bend angle as changing resistance A game controller that reads button states, thumbstick positions, and rumble signals Notice that microphone, webcam, and Kinect are in that list. They are sensors too! What about computer vision — does it count? If you're using a webcam with software like MediaPipe, Wekinator, or OpenPose to extract gesture, pose, or facial landmarks, you're running a sensor and an interpretation layer on top of it. The sensor (webcam) reads raw pixel data. The model reads that data and outputs a higher-order description (hand position, skeletal angle, detected emotion). Both layers involve reduction and both layers are legitimate sites of creative and critical inquiry. The question to ask is: what does the model's interpretation assume about bodies, movement, and legibility? Who was the training data? Whose gesture gets read cleanly, and whose doesn't? An early pain point, as we have discovered together, is in approaching physical computing for the first time by starting with the sensor. So lets work backwards to the sensors starting with the thinking and curiosity!Working in this order will help keep your practice in the driver's seat. The sensor becomes an epistemic tool you've chosen for a reason.If your practice is drawn to movement, gesture, dance, or the body in space: → You're probably interested in orientation, acceleration, or spatial position data → Consider: IMU/accelerometer/gyroscope (Stemma QT options: LSM6DS3, LSM9DS1, BNO055), depth camera (Kinect, Intel RealSense), MediaPipe pose estimation via webcam
If your practice is drawn to touch, contact, material surfaces, textile, or skin: → You're probably interested in discrete contact events, pressure, or capacitance data → Consider: MPR121 capacitive touch (Stemma QT), FSR (force-sensitive resistors, any), piezoelectric transducers, velostat/conductive fabric
If your practice is drawn to sound, voice, sonic environment, acoustic space: → You're probably interested in amplitude, frequency content, onset events, or spectral shape → Consider: electret microphone + breakout, MEMS microphone (Stemma QT: PDM microphone), field recorders into audio analysis software, FFT in Max/MSP or TouchDesigner
If your practice is drawn to proximity, presence, or environmental sensing: → You're probably interested in distance, occupancy, or ambient conditions (temperature, light, humidity) → Consider: VL53L1X time-of-flight (Stemma QT), APDS-9960 proximity + color (Stemma QT), PIR motion sensor, thermal camera (AMG8833 grid-eye, Stemma QT)
If your practice is drawn to biological states (stress, arousal, breath, heartbeat): → You're probably interested in physiological signals as data (GSR, pulse, respiration, heat rate) → Consider: GSR sensor + voltage divider, MAX30102 pulse oximeter (Stemma QT), piezo on chest or wrist for breath/heartbeat, stretch sensor
Not an exhaustive list of pathways, but it is a start!Before we discuss specific hardware purchases or setups, answer these questions. Write them in your Critical Technical Journal if you’d like, or bring them as notes to discuss in class or in a message to me (the instructor). 1. What is your practice thinking about right now? Not what you want to make — what is your practice interested in? What questions, materials, bodies, phenomena, histories, or tensions keep pulling your attention? 2. What are you curious about in terms of physical phenomena? Movement? Contact? Sound? Environmental change? Biological states? Something else? More than one thing is fine. 3. What kinds of data would let you work with those phenomena? Try to be specific. Not "sensor data," but what kind of data? A stream of numbers? Threshold events (on/off)? A spatial map? A frequency spectrum? 4. Make a list. Based on your answers above, write a rough list of the types of data you think you need. Don't worry yet about whether a sensor exists for it. Just name what you want to know about the physical world. Once you have that list, we can map it to available sensors, identify what's accessible via Stemma QT / Qwiic, and figure out a reasonable path for your practice project.If you need to purchase sensors:
Adafruit (adafruit.com): primary source for Stemma QT ecosystem. Use the "Stemma QT" filter in their sensors category.
SparkFun (sparkfun.com): Qwiic ecosystem, fully compatible. Digikey / Mouser: for bulk or harder-to-find parts; more intimidating but comprehensive. Check the BB Lear site under /Resources/Shopping for Sensors/ for more useful info!If cost is a barrier, talk to the instructor before purchasing anything.

digm-553/week-01-practice-immanent-criti.title: (Im)material Potluck — Preparation
digm-553/week-01-practice-immanent-criti.description:
Due: Week 02 - Bring your contribution to class. This is part of ASN 1: Potluck + Speculative Proposal.The (Im)material Potluck is a collective opening ritual for the course. Each student brings one thing — physical or immaterial — to contribute to a shared conversation about material, tools, and practice. It is as much a show-and-tell as it is an opening proposition.Consider the object you bring is an argument. It says something about your practice, your research, your questions. Your job is to be able to articulate what argument yours is making. Your contribution can be physical or immaterial, hence (im)material. What it cannot be is arbitrary. It should be something with stakes for your own work.Physical examples: A material you keep returning to (fabric, copper tape, wood, clay, wire) A piece of hardware that has shaped how you think (a sensor, a circuit board, a connector, an old device) An object from your research environment (something from a site you've been working in) A tool that frustrates you in productive ways Immaterial examples: A dataset, protocol, or schema you work with A sound or sound file (something you've recorded or that recurs in your practice) A constraint or rule you've imposed on yourself An image, a diagram, a piece of notation A system or process (something that has no single physical form) If your contribution is immaterial, come ready to share it on screen/speakers or describe it precisely. Vagueness is not the same as immateriality.For each contribution, you'll have a few minutes to speak (~5min). Prepare to address:1. Why this thing? Not its origin story — the practical reason it has stakes in your work. What does this object or material make possible in your practice that other things don't? What does working with it feel like, and what does that feeling tell you? 2. What does it open? What questions does it raise that you can't yet answer? What does it put into contact with other things in your work? Where does it lead?3. What is it thinking? Manning & Massumi: "Every practice is a mode of thought, already in the act." Objects and materials are part of practices: they aren't passive. What mode of thought is already active in the thing you're bringing? What does it do to the practice it's part of — not just what you do with it, but what it does to you? You don't need fully formed answers. You need to have asked the questions and be willing to sit with them in the room.The reading assigned this week is useful preparation for how to think about your object before you bring it. A few entry points:Manning & Massumi: They distinguish between framing (setting up a structure in advance) and conditioning (bringing co-causes into interaction to produce emergence). Is your object a frame or a condition? What does it enable that you didn't design in advance? There is no size or format requirement. One thing is enough. If it's fragile, pack accordingly. If it's large, photograph it and bring the photo plus a fragment. If it's truly immaterial and screen-sharing is difficult, prepare a 30-second verbal description precise enough that the room can hold it. You will not be graded on the quality of the object, only on the specificity and honesty of how you speak about it (plus your reflection post on it as well! ).

digm-553/week-01-practice-immanent-criti.title: Reading Guide — Week 01
digm-553/week-01-practice-immanent-criti.description:
Primary reading due Week 02. Background readings recommended before or alongside class. Propositions 0–3 (pp. 83–97) Minnesota University Press, 2014.Access: Manning + Massumi – Though in the ActDo not try to understand this text completely on a first read. For context, these are two authors who think that the form of writing itself should enact the argument being made; so it is written as such. It also may read as a bit “overly critical,” but it is important to understanding the context of their work. Let the reading wash over you once. Then read it again more slowly, with a highlighter or notebook.On the first pass: Mark any sentence that feels like it's writing about your own practice, even if you can't yet say why. Don't worry about the vocabulary.On the second pass: Look for these three things specifically: The word technique and how they're using it The distinction between conditioning and framing Any moment where they talk about what a body does (including a digital body) These are not quiz questions! Just points of entry to the conversation; points of inquiry and immobility, both. You need not provide written answers, but you should have, at least, thought about them. Manning & Massumi say research-creation happens at the "prebifurcation point", a point before research and creation diverge into institutional structures. Where is that point in your current practice? Is there a moment in your workflow when the thinking and the making are still the same thing? When does the split happen? They distinguish between framing a project (setting up a structure in advance) and conditioning one (bringing co-causes into interaction so something can emerge). Think of a project you've worked on. Was it framed or conditioned, maybe even both, at different stages? What did that feel like from the inside? "An enabling constraint is positive in its dynamic effect, even though it may be limiting in its form." What enabling constraints are already active in your tools, materials, and methods? Which ones do you want to be more deliberate about? "Unconstrained interaction rarely yields worthwhile effects." Do you agree? What is the minimum constraint needed for something interesting to happen in your practice? Manning & Massumi warn against research-creation settling into "a communication model revolving around the delivery of results." How does your current program or discipline evaluate your work? Where does that evaluation model push back against research-creation? You don't need to have fully digested any of this before Week 02. You need to: Have read Manning & Massumi Propositions 0–3 at least once
Have your (Im)material Potluck contribution ready: see (Im)material Potluck — Prep Have at least one question or point of friction from the reading to bring into the room The discussions are only as good as what each person brings to it. Your confusion is just as valuable as your insight, so bring both! :)

digm-553/week-01-practice-immanent-criti.title: Epistemic Tools Introduction
digm-553/week-01-practice-immanent-criti.description:
"Instruments have a life of their own. They do not merely follow theory; often they determine theory, because instruments determine what is possible, and what is possible determines to a large extent what can be thought." — Hankins & Silverman, quoted in Magnusson If W01Aestablished research-creation as the methodological orientation of this course, This section (W01B) establishes the epistemic status of the tools you work with.These two moves are connected: if making is already a mode of thinking, then the instrument you make with is already shaping the kinds of thought that are possible.This is what Magnusson, following Hankins & Silverman and Don Ihde, means by epistemic tools: instruments are not passive, nor neutral. Instruments (artistic, musical, scientific, or otherwise) act as active participants in the construction of knowledge. The choice of what instrument to use is also not neutral. It conditions what questions you can ask, what results you can produce, and, eventually, what can be considered beautiful, interesting, or true.For us, this puts our tool choices in a new light. Choosing TouchDesigner over Processing, Max/MSP over SuperCollider, a capacitive sensor over a camera are all epistemological decisions as much as they are technical ones.Don Ihde identified four phenomenological modalities of instrument-use. We will look at the three most prominent ways that instruments mediate between the body and the world:You act through the instrument, which extends your body or amplifies your senses. The instrument recedes into the background (the hidden 4th relation - Background Relations). You experience through and with technology, not at a technology. A well-practiced keyboard player doesn't think about the keys; they think about the music. The keys are an extension of the hand.The instrument produces data that you must interpret. A spectrograph, a heat map, an oscilloscope reading. The instrument mediates reality by translating it into a representation via abstractions, but that representation requires interpretive work to become knowledge.The instrument becomes something you engage with for its own sake, as a “quasi-other”, a presence with its own agency. Virtual reality headsets, interactive installations, or a generative system that responds to you all produce this kind of relation.Important These modalities should not be considered exclusive categories. Think of them more as tendencies. Any given practice involves mixtures and oscillations between them. And they are not value-neutral: each modality shapes what you notice, what you miss, and what you expect the instrument to do for you. One of Don Ihde's most directly practical insight: every instrument involves amplification-reduction transformations. It amplifies certain features of the world and reduces others. And there is no exception to this.One important question to always ask of a tool, technology, or model is: “What is gained and what is lost when I apply it?” A microphone (through a purely physical model/definition) amplifies pressure-wave events in a certain frequency ranges (based on it circuit design and construction) and reduces everything else. A MIDI controller amplifies discrete pitch/velocity events and reduces continuous, gestural sound. A capacitive touch sensor amplifies conductivity at specific points and reduces everything that isn't electrical contact. The danger is not that [tools/technologies/models/definitions] reduce. All of them do to some extent. The danger is forgetting that they do. When the reduction becomes invisible, the thing not being captured disappears from your thinking entirely.Magnusson on software: Musical software encodes inherited defaults: equal-tempered tuning, temporal quantization, note-based event models. But they aren’t musical “facts” or “truths” and they seldom capture the full range of musical expression. What they are contingent historical choices that have been naturalized through adoption (sometimes forced) and repeated use in which what was reduced has faded away. They have become what Latour (and Bowker & Star) call black boxes. A black box is an object or system whose internal workings have become invisible through repeated use. Latour: "objects establish themselves as black boxes through repeated use and in the process their origins disappear." Bowker and Star extend this: "the more naturalized the object becomes, the more unquestioning the relationship of the community to it; the more invisible the contingent and historical circumstances of its birth, the more it sinks into the community's routinely forgotten memory." Take note on what this means for practice: the tools you're most fluent with are the most dangerous. Fluency produces blindness. The instrument you've used for years is the instrument whose assumptions you've most thoroughly absorbed into your practice without noticing. Critical technical Practice (CTP) connection: This is why what Agre describes as the "split identity" matters. One foot in craft, one foot in critique. The craft foot needs fluency. The critique foot needs to keep opening the black boxes that fluency keeps closing.Philip Agre's phrase points to a specific version of “computational imperialism”: computers "aim to reinvent virtually every other site of practice in its own image." They are built from representational models and abstractions of the activities they will be used to perform. However, in doing so, But they also restructure those activities, fundamentally. Example A digital audio workstation (DAW) doesn't just record and edit audio. It restructures the practice of making music around the concept of a timeline, discrete regions, channels, effects chains, automation curves, etc… This perpetuates a model of music-making built by engineers with particular assumptions about what music is. A computer, then, does not simply have an instrumental use in a given site of practice; the computer is frequently about that site in its very design.This is why Agre says that technical people often experience phenomenological texts as "sounding like mysticism." The mismatch in philosophy and understanding exists because the computer's representational model and the phenomenologist's model of experience are genuinely incommensurable. digm-553/week-01-practice-immanent-criti.description:
"The digital system is material in its body, electric in function, and symbolic in control." — Magnusson, Sonic Writing You could read this note as a checklist of tools we might be using this term. But given what we've spent W01A and W01B establishing that tools are epistemic, that instruments condition what can be thought, that amplification is always also reduction. Well, we can't rightly do that with a straight face, can we?Instead, consider this an epistemic inventory. For each element of the course toolkit, we'll be asking: what does this tool make possible, what does it foreclose, and why did we choose it?The physical-digital entanglement at the center of this course runs through a specific signal chain (maybe not this specifically, but something similar):Body / Material World ↓ MPR121 Sensor (capacitive touch) ↓ Adafruit QT Py RP2040 (microcontroller) ↓ CircuitPython (embedded code) ↓ OSC / UDP (protocol over Wi-Fi) ↓ TouchDesigner / Max/MSP / Ableton (host software) ↓ Sound, Image, Data Output Each arrow in this chain is a transformation. Each of those transformations amplifies something and also reduces something else. The QT Py RP2040 is a small microcontroller board built around the Raspberry Pi RP2040 chip. It runs CircuitPython a version of Python designed for embedded systems with limited memory and no operating system. Or it can also run Arduino or PlatformIO both versions of C++ for embedded systems. Why this board, epistemically?The QT Py is small enough to embed in an object, a garment, or a physical installation. We couldn’t do that with a desktop PC. So, this changes the relationship between the body and the computation. The computation moves toward the body rather than the body moving toward the computation. This also presents a design decision with consequences for what kind of physical-digital entanglement is possible.It also has explicit constraints: limited memory, no file system (without an SD card), no display, no persistent storage across power cycles. These are enabling constraints. They push us toward thinking about computation as a real-time process happening in a physical context, not a processing pipeline running on a workstation, rendered, then presented.Ihde's modalities here: In typical use, the microcontroller operates in a hermeneutic relation, meaning it produces data (sensor readings) that you then interpret in software. But as your fluency develops, it can shift toward an embodiment relation, where the hardware/body interface recedes and you're thinking directly in terms of interaction rather than data.The MPR121 detects electrical conductance at 12 separate electrode points. When a conductive object (a finger, a body part, water, conductive thread, foil, fruit, etc.) comes near or touches an electrode, the sensor registers a change in capacitance.Epistemic specifics:The MPR121 models the world as twelve discrete contact points with threshold values. It does not model pressure, velocity, texture, or gesture in any richer sense. This is a fairly substantial reduction, but also a generative constraint.Why 12? A speculative aside on hardware and tonality The MPR121's 12-electrode architecture is almost certainly a pragmatic engineering choice. 12 is a highly composite number, divisible by 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, and 12 — which makes it a natural Schelling point in design: enough channels for most multi-touch applications, manageable over I2C, and culturally unremarkable. We already organise time in 12s (months, hours (non-24)), commerce in 12s (dozens, gross), and space in 12s (inches to the foot). All this to say, the number doesn't need music theory to justify itself. But the coincidence is worth sitting with, I think: 12 also happens to map cleanly onto the chromatic scale of Western 12-tone equal temperament. A person who assigns one pitch per electrode isn't fighting the hardware. They'd working with a latent affordance the chip happens to carry. Whether that affordance was designed or accidental doesn't change the fact that it's there, and that it quietly favors a particular musical cosmology over others. The epistemic question it opens: what would a 19-electrode sensor do to your compositional assumptions? What practices would suddenly feel natural, and whose tuning systems, microtonal, spectral, non-Western, would feel less like workarounds? What this reduction enables: you have to build gestural richness out of combination, sequencing, timing, and creative use of what "electrode" means materially. The sensor touching a piece of copper tape embedded in a textile or paper is not the same experience as touching a pad on a breakout board, even if the the electrical signal may be identical.The sensor does not care about the materiality of what it touches. That indifference is the limitation. Making that indifference expressive is the research-creation challenge.The Zoom H5 is a portable, mid-range field recorder. Four inputs (two XLR combo jacks, plus the built-in X/Y capsule pair), 24-32bit/96kHz recording, small enough to carry anywhere.Epistemic framing: The H5 models the world as microphone placements and headroom. Unlike software recording, field recording asks you to solve problems in space and time before you can solve them in software. You can't EQ a bad room placement (kinda). The recorder forces decisions about where you are and where the sound is in a way that a software sampler does not.The H5 is also a tool for practice-based research: documentation, listening, locating yourself in a sonic environment. Used as a research tool (not just a production tool), it is a way of attending to a space before you decide what to make there.CircuitPython is Python stripped down for embedded environments. The key constraint: no concurrency, no threads, single-threaded event loop. Your code runs top to bottom, repeatedly, in a tight main loop.Epistemic consequence: You cannot think about this system the way you think about desktop software. There is no background thread listening for events while the foreground does something else. Everything is sequential. This forces particular models of time, interaction, and performance. Actually, one that is closer to how musical performance works (step by step, no stopping) than how most software development works.The loop structure also makes the code's relationship to time explicit. The latency between sensing and responding is determined by how much work you do in each loop iteration. You feel computation as time.OSC is a protocol originally designed for real-time communication between musical instruments and software. It uses the UDP networking protocol, which means messages are sent in discrete packets that can arrive out of order or not at all. It is a protocol that prioritizes low latency over guaranteed delivery.Epistemic framing: OSC messages have a specific structure: an address pattern (like /sensor/touch/1) and typed arguments. This structure makes the musical/physical origin of the data visible in the data itself. Unlike MIDI, which was designed around keyboard-and-note-number logic, OSC is relatively free, the address namespace is whatever you define.The UDP choice (vs. TCP) is itself an argument about what matters: latency matters more than reliability. For real-time physical interaction, a dropped packet is usually less harmful than a 50ms delay. This is a design philosophy embedded in the computation and protocol.TouchDesigner is a node-based visual programming environment developed by Derivative, used widely for real-time visual performance, interactive installations, and physical computing. It receives OSC messages (among may other protocols like DMX, MIDI, etc.), processes them in a dataflow graph, and routes the results to visual, audio, or other outputs.Epistemic specifics:TouchDesigner models the world as a cooking system: operators (nodes) either cook (update their output) or don't, based on whether their inputs have changed. This is a specific model of reactive computation, and it is one that is very well suited for real-time visual work and less natural for sequential or text-based logic.The node-based paradigm also has an epistemological consequence: your decisions are made visible as connections. You can see the shape of your logic. This is different from writing code in an IDE, where the structure of your reasoning is embedded in and enabled by syntax. The defaults matter here (returning to Magnusson): the built-in operators in TouchDesigner assume certain things about color, resolution, framerate, and timing that reflect the tool's origins in VVVV and cinema-influenced real-time graphics. When you use those defaults without questioning them, you're (perhaps subconsciously) making an implicit argument about what your work should look like.Max/MSP (and its twin PureData) are the older cousins of TouchDesigner. They are node-based environments with deeper roots in algorithmic musical composition and signal processing. Where TouchDesigner is GPU-native and optimized for visual output, Max is CPU-native and optimized for audio, MIDI, and raw numerical data.Why both? The choice between TouchDesigner and Max is not always a purely technical one. Often times, it is partly a question of disciplinary genealogy. TouchDesigner comes from the VJ / visual performance world; Max comes from the electroacoustic music world. They carry different assumptions about what a "performance" is, what "real-time" means, and what relationship between software and body is natural.Using both is an opportunity to feel those differences in your body as you work and to make that felt for anyone interacting with your work.Here is the exercise this note is preparing you for:Do your own epistemic inventory. Pick tool(s) you already use in your practice, any tool(s) really, not necessarily the ones listed here. For each one: What does it amplify? (What becomes easy, visible, measurable?) What does it reduce? (What disappears, becomes invisible, gets rounded off?) What world does it assume exists? (What is the implicit model of activity, interaction, body, material that its design encodes?) Who designed those assumptions, and for what context? digm-553/week-01-practice-immanent-criti.description:
"Making would already be thinking-in-action, and conceptualization a practice in its own right." — Manning & Massumi, Thought in the Act Most of what we call "research" and most of what we call "creative practice" assume they are separate, sequential, activities. Research produces knowledge. Then, practice produces work. The knowledge informs the work. The work illustrates the knowledge. This is the typical “institutional model” of knowledge production. It is also the model we're going to spend the rest of this course systematically inhabiting and turning.Research-creation, as described by the authors Manning & Massumi is an activity that occurs at what they call the prebifurcation point : the point just before research and creation diverge into the institutional structures that evaluate them by separate criteria. At that point, making and thinking are not distinct acts. They are two registers of the same act, happening simultaneously.The theme of Week 01 is "Practice Immanent Critique." Here's what that phrase means from the ground up.An immanent critique does not stand outside a system to pass judgment. Instead, it works from inside. Id does so in order to inhabit the structure, understand its logic from within, and then find the pressure points where it might be turned. Manning & Massumi's definition:"An immanent critique engages with new processes more than new products, from a constructivist angle. It seeks to energize new modes of activity, already in germ, that seem to offer a potential to escape or overspill ready-made channelings into the dominant value system. The strategy of immanent critique is to inhabit one's complicity and make it turn — in the sense in which butter 'turns' to curd."Notice what this requires: inhabiting complicity. You are not exempt from the system you critique. You work from within it, on its tools, in its institutions, using its grants and its grades. Immanent critique means doing that while turning it, not waiting until you're free of it to begin this form of practice.So, let’s analyze this from our shared perspective. For this course: We are working at a university. We use tools (TouchDesigner, Max/MSP, Ableton, Python) that carry embedded worldviews. We receive grades. All of this is our complicity. Immanent critique is the method by which we make that complicity productive rather than just reproductive.Manning & Massumi acknowledge a tension: the institutional framing of research-creation — especially in the context of digital media and media studies — pushes it toward "formatting artistic activity for more directly economic forms of delivery to stakeholders." Digital media works often get funded in part because they "employ the same technological platforms as the increasingly computerized economy."For us, this is a friction of our practice (and a contradiction that is not easily resolved). Our work is to neither ignore this friction nor be paralyzed by it. Instead we should treat it as what Agre would call a hassle: a recurring friction that is itself data about the structure of the field.The danger Manning & Massumi identify: research-creation "settles into a communication model revolving around the delivery of results." The goal instead is what they call "an interpenetration of processes rather than a communication of products."What does that mean in practice? When you work on a project in this course, you are not primarily building something that will be assessed. You are practicing something. Developing a relationship to your tools, your materials, and your questions. The artifact becomes secondary, it is the record of that practice, not the point of it.These are technically different acts. Framing is setting up a structure: here are the rules, here are the constraints, here is the question, go. Conditioning is bringing co-causes into interaction such that something emerges that neither cause alone would produce. "Conditioning consists in bringing co-causes into interaction, such that the participation yields something different from either acting alone… Emergent process, dedicated to the singular occurrence of the new, agitates inventively in an open field. Programmed organization, on the other hand, functions predictably in a bounded frame and lends itself to reproduction."In this class, we are going to try to condition rather than frame. We should strive to set up initial conditions; not attempt to predetermine outcomes.The concept that connects it all: enabling constraints.An enabling constraint is positive in its dynamic effect even though it may be limiting in its form. The classic example: gravity is a constraint on dance, but it enables the jump. Without gravity to push against, there is no arc, no lift, no landing. The jump is a collaboration between the dancer and gravity — two co-causes whose interaction produces something neither does alone."In our experience, unconstrained interaction rarely yields worthwhile effects."This applies directly to the hardware and software in this course. The MPR121 sensor constrains what counts as input. CircuitPython constrains what you can compute on the microcontroller. OSC protocol constrains the format of the data. These are not obstacles — they are the material conditions out of which something emerges. The question is not how to eliminate constraints but how to turn them from limitative to enabling.Manning & Massumi introduce the concept of techniques of relation: "devices for catalyzing and modulating interaction" that comprise "a domain of practice in their own right." Techniques of relation are are structural: they shape how things interact, how processes co-evolve, how different elements of a practice can be brought into productive contact. They operate in two modes: Techniques that set up initial conditions — propitious starting points for emergence Techniques that modulate an event as it moves through its phases — improvised steering without predetermined destination A key property: "Techniques as we understand them do not depend exclusively on the content of the practices but move across their respective processes at the site of their potential multiplication." A technique is transferable. It can move from sound to movement to code to pedagogy.Assignment connection: Part of your ASN 2 (Critical Technical Journal) practice is to identify the techniques of relation already operating in your practice in order to begin consciously designing new ones.If every practice is already a mode of thought, what is your current practice thinking?Manning & Massumi open Thought in the Act with: "Every practice is a mode of thought, already in the act. To dance: a thinking in movement. To paint: a thinking through color. To perceive in the everyday: a thinking of the world's varied ways of affording itself."So for us: To program is a thinking in what? To route audio signals is a thinking in what? To touch a capacitive sensor is a thinking in what? To capture field recordings is a thinking in what? Right now, these are more rhetorical questions, but your first journal entries will begin to answer them, literally. Research-creation — activity at the prebifurcation point where making and thinking are co-constitutive, not sequential Immanent critique — inhabiting complicity and making it turn; critique from inside, not outside Enabling constraint — a limitation that, through interaction with other forces, generates emergence rather than just restriction Conditioning — bringing co-causes into interaction toward open, emergent outcomes (vs. framing toward predetermined ones) Techniques of relation — devices for catalyzing and modulating interaction; transferable across practices Manning + Massumi — Thought in the Act (Propositions 0–3, pp. 83–97)

You can see the shape of your logic. This is different from writing code in an IDE, where the structure of your reasoning is embedded in and enabled by syntax. The defaults matter here (returning to Magnusson): the built-in operators in TouchDesigner assume certain things about color, resolution, framerate, and timing that reflect the tool's origins in VVVV and cinema-influenced real-time graphics. When you use those defaults without questioning them, you're (perhaps subconsciously) making an implicit argument about what your work should look like.Max/MSP (and its twin PureData) are the older cousins of TouchDesigner. They are node-based environments with deeper roots in algorithmic musical composition and signal processing. Where TouchDesigner is GPU-native and optimized for visual output, Max is CPU-native and optimized for audio, MIDI, and raw numerical data.Why both? The choice between TouchDesigner and Max is not always a purely technical one. Often times, it is partly a question of disciplinary genealogy. TouchDesigner comes from the VJ / visual performance world; Max comes from the electroacoustic music world. They carry different assumptions about what a "performance" is, what "real-time" means, and what relationship between software and body is natural.Using both is an opportunity to feel those differences in your body as you work and to make that felt for anyone interacting with your work.Here is the exercise this note is preparing you for:Do your own epistemic inventory. What does it reduce? (What disappears, becomes invisible, gets rounded off?) What world does it assume exists? Research produces knowledge. Then, practice produces work. The knowledge informs the work. The work illustrates the knowledge. This is the typical “institutional model” of knowledge production. It is also the model we're going to spend the rest of this course systematically inhabiting and turning.Research-creation, as described by the authors Manning & Massumi is an activity that occurs at what they call the prebifurcation point : the point just before research and creation diverge into the institutional structures that evaluate them by separate criteria. At that point, making and thinking are not distinct acts. They are two registers of the same act, happening simultaneously.The theme of Week 01 is "Practice Immanent Critique." Here's what that phrase means from the ground up.An immanent critique does not stand outside a system to pass judgment. Instead, it works from inside. Id does so in order to inhabit the structure, understand its logic from within, and then find the pressure points where it might be turned. Manning & Massumi's definition:"An immanent critique engages with new processes more than new products, from a constructivist angle. It seeks to energize new modes of activity, already in germ, that seem to offer a potential to escape or overspill ready-made channelings into the dominant value system. The strategy of immanent critique is to inhabit one's complicity and make it turn — in the sense in which butter 'turns' to curd."Notice what this requires: inhabiting complicity. You are not exempt from the system you critique. You work from within it, on its tools, in its institutions, using its grants and its grades. Immanent critique means doing that while turning it, not waiting until you're free of it to begin this form of practice.So, let’s analyze this from our shared perspective. For this course: We are working at a university. We use tools (TouchDesigner, Max/MSP, Ableton, Python) that carry embedded worldviews. We receive grades. All of this is our complicity. Immanent critique is the method by which we make that complicity productive rather than just reproductive.Manning & Massumi acknowledge a tension: the institutional framing of research-creation — especially in the context of digital media and media studies — pushes it toward "formatting artistic activity for more directly economic forms of delivery to stakeholders." Digital media works often get funded in part because they "employ the same technological platforms as the increasingly computerized economy."For us, this is a friction of our practice (and a contradiction that is not easily resolved). Our work is to neither ignore this friction nor be paralyzed by it. Instead we should treat it as what Agre would call a hassle: a recurring friction that is itself data about the structure of the field.The danger Manning & Massumi identify: research-creation "settles into a communication model revolving around the delivery of results." The goal instead is what they call "an interpenetration of processes rather than a communication of products."What does that mean in practice? When you work on a project in this course, you are not primarily building something that will be assessed. You are practicing something. Developing a relationship to your tools, your materials, and your questions. The artifact becomes secondary, it is the record of that practice, not the point of it.These are technically different acts. Framing is setting up a structure: here are the rules, here are the constraints, here is the question, go. Conditioning is bringing co-causes into interaction such that something emerges that neither cause alone would produce. "Conditioning consists in bringing co-causes into interaction, such that the participation yields something different from either acting alone… Emergent process, dedicated to the singular occurrence of the new, agitates inventively in an open field. Programmed organization, on the other hand, functions predictably in a bounded frame and lends itself to reproduction."In this class, we are going to try to condition rather than frame. We should strive to set up initial conditions; not attempt to predetermine outcomes.The concept that connects it all: enabling constraints.An enabling constraint is positive in its dynamic effect even though it may be limiting in its form. The classic example: gravity is a constraint on dance, but it enables the jump. Without gravity to push against, there is no arc, no lift, no landing. The jump is a collaboration between the dancer and gravity — two co-causes whose interaction produces something neither does alone."In our experience, unconstrained interaction rarely yields worthwhile effects."This applies directly to the hardware and software in this course. The MPR121 sensor constrains what counts as input. CircuitPython constrains what you can compute on the microcontroller. OSC protocol constrains the format of the data. These are not obstacles — they are the material conditions out of which something emerges. The question is not how to eliminate constraints but how to turn them from limitative to enabling.Manning & Massumi introduce the concept of techniques of relation: "devices for catalyzing and modulating interaction" that comprise "a domain of practice in their own right." Techniques of relation are are structural: they shape how things interact, how processes co-evolve, how different elements of a practice can be brought into productive contact. They operate in two modes: Techniques that set up initial conditions — propitious starting points for emergence Techniques that modulate an event as it moves through its phases — improvised steering without predetermined destination A key property: "Techniques as we understand them do not depend exclusively on the content of the practices but move across their respective processes at the site of their potential multiplication." A technique is transferable. It can move from sound to movement to code to pedagogy.Assignment connection: Part of your ASN 2 (Critical Technical Journal) practice is to identify the techniques of relation already operating in your practice in order to begin consciously designing new ones.If every practice is already a mode of thought, what is your current practice thinking?Manning & Massumi open Thought in the Act with: "Every practice is a mode of thought, already in the act. To dance: a thinking in movement. To paint: a thinking through color. To perceive in the everyday: a thinking of the world's varied ways of affording itself."So for us: To program is a thinking in what? To route audio signals is a thinking in what? To touch a capacitive sensor is a thinking in what? To capture field recordings is a thinking in what? Right now, these are more rhetorical questions, but your first journal entries will begin to answer them, literally. If W01Aestablished research-creation as the methodological orientation of this course, This section (W01B) establishes the epistemic status of the tools you work with.These two moves are connected: if making is already a mode of thinking, then the instrument you make with is already shaping the kinds of thought that are possible.This is what Magnusson, following Hankins & Silverman and Don Ihde, means by epistemic tools: instruments are not passive, nor neutral. Instruments (artistic, musical, scientific, or otherwise) act as active participants in the construction of knowledge. The choice of what instrument to use is also not neutral. It conditions what questions you can ask, what results you can produce, and, eventually, what can be considered beautiful, interesting, or true.For us, this puts our tool choices in a new light. Choosing TouchDesigner over Processing, Max/MSP over SuperCollider, a capacitive sensor over a camera are all epistemological decisions as much as they are technical ones.Don Ihde identified four phenomenological modalities of instrument-use. We will look at the three most prominent ways that instruments mediate between the body and the world:You act through the instrument, which extends your body or amplifies your senses. The instrument recedes into the background (the hidden 4th relation - Background Relations). You experience through and with technology, not at a technology. A well-practiced keyboard player doesn't think about the keys; they think about the music. The keys are an extension of the hand.The instrument produces data that you must interpret. A spectrograph, a heat map, an oscilloscope reading. The instrument mediates reality by translating it into a representation via abstractions, but that representation requires interpretive work to become knowledge.The instrument becomes something you engage with for its own sake, as a “quasi-other”, a presence with its own agency. Virtual reality headsets, interactive installations, or a generative system that responds to you all produce this kind of relation.Important These modalities should not be considered exclusive categories. Think of them more as tendencies. Any given practice involves mixtures and oscillations between them. And they are not value-neutral: each modality shapes what you notice, what you miss, and what you expect the instrument to do for you. One of Don Ihde's most directly practical insight: every instrument involves amplification-reduction transformations. It amplifies certain features of the world and reduces others. And there is no exception to this.One important question to always ask of a tool, technology, or model is: “What is gained and what is lost when I apply it?” A microphone (through a purely physical model/definition) amplifies pressure-wave events in a certain frequency ranges (based on it circuit design and construction) and reduces everything else. A MIDI controller amplifies discrete pitch/velocity events and reduces continuous, gestural sound. A capacitive touch sensor amplifies conductivity at specific points and reduces everything that isn't electrical contact. The danger is not that [tools/technologies/models/definitions] reduce. All of them do to some extent. The danger is forgetting that they do. When the reduction becomes invisible, the thing not being captured disappears from your thinking entirely.Magnusson on software: Musical software encodes inherited defaults: equal-tempered tuning, temporal quantization, note-based event models. But they aren’t musical “facts” or “truths” and they seldom capture the full range of musical expression. What they are contingent historical choices that have been naturalized through adoption (sometimes forced) and repeated use in which what was reduced has faded away. They have become what Latour (and Bowker & Star) call black boxes. A black box is an object or system whose internal workings have become invisible through repeated use. Latour: "objects establish themselves as black boxes through repeated use and in the process their origins disappear." Bowker and Star extend this: "the more naturalized the object becomes, the more unquestioning the relationship of the community to it; the more invisible the contingent and historical circumstances of its birth, the more it sinks into the community's routinely forgotten memory." Take note on what this means for practice: the tools you're most fluent with are the most dangerous. Fluency produces blindness. The instrument you've used for years is the instrument whose assumptions you've most thoroughly absorbed into your practice without noticing. Critical technical Practice (CTP) connection: This is why what Agre describes as the "split identity" matters. One foot in craft, one foot in critique. The craft foot needs fluency. The critique foot needs to keep opening the black boxes that fluency keeps closing.Philip Agre's phrase points to a specific version of “computational imperialism”: computers "aim to reinvent virtually every other site of practice in its own image." They are built from representational models and abstractions of the activities they will be used to perform. However, in doing so, But they also restructure those activities, fundamentally. Example A digital audio workstation (DAW) doesn't just record and edit audio. It restructures the practice of making music around the concept of a timeline, discrete regions, channels, effects chains, automation curves, etc… This perpetuates a model of music-making built by engineers with particular assumptions about what music is. A computer, then, does not simply have an instrumental use in a given site of practice; the computer is frequently about that site in its very design.This is why Agre says that technical people often experience phenomenological texts as "sounding like mysticism." The mismatch in philosophy and understanding exists because the computer's representational model and the phenomenologist's model of experience are genuinely incommensurable. You can't translate one into the other because they aren't the same kind of thing. Agre's solution: stop translating, start learning on their (meaning models and practice of phenomenological experiences) own terms.Thor Magnusson in ‘‘Sonic Writing” spins a particular historical framing of a driving problem this way: Western philosophy has long separated techne (making, craft, technique) from episteme (knowledge, theory, science). Instruments of art were not instruments of knowledge; skill was not wisdom.In more modern theory and practice, this separation is now being productively challenged: by cognitive science (embodied cognition, enactivism) by STS (Science and Technology Studies) by research-creation methodology by practitioners in new interfaces for musical expression, interactive art, and critical making. IN doing so, our instruments become epistemic, fusing instrument with composition, as in the works of Gordon Mumma, David Tudor, and other practitioners and disciplines. The digital system is, as Magnusson puts it, "material in its body, electric in function, and symbolic in control." All three registers are active all at once.Three questions to hold as you work through this course:What does your tool amplify? What aspects of your practice does it make easier to see, hear, measure, or manipulate? What does your tool reduce? What is systematically missing from what your tool captures? What can't it represent How has the above shaped what you've been making? Who designed the magnification-reduction? The defaults in your software were chosen by someone with specific assumptions. What were those assumptions, and whose experience of the world did they take as universally applicable? The course structure itself is an attempt to condition otherwise.🔴 Theory — Definition: "An enabling constraint is positive in its dynamic effect, even though it may be limiting in its form/force narrowly considered."🔴 Theory — Conditioning vs. framing: "Conditioning consists in bringing co-causes into interaction, such that the participation yields something different from either acting alone… Emergent process, dedicated to the singular occurrence of the new, agitates inventively in an open field. Programmed organization, on the other hand, functions predictably in a bounded frame and lends itself to reproduction."🔵 Project Hook — Gravity/dance example: The jump: gravity is implaccable, but add horizontal movement and "the arc of the jump will be a collaboration between the action of gravity and the energy and angular momentum of the horizontal movement acting as co-causes." Gravity converts from limitative to enabling constraint. → What is the "gravity" in your media system? The hardware constraints, the protocol limitations, the material resistance of your chosen tools?🟢 Pedagogic — Assignment connection: Students will design their own "techniques of relation — devices for catalyzing and modulating interaction." These techniques must "implant opportunities for creative participation, which would be encouraged to take on their own shape, direction, and momentum." → Links directly to ASN 2 (Critical Technical Journal) and ASN 3 (Experimental Media Project).🔴 Theory — Two kinds of technique: Techniques to set in place propitious initial conditions Techniques to modulate the event as it moves through its phases 🔵 Project Hook — Techniques are agnostic: "Techniques as we understand them do not depend exclusively on the content of the practices but move across their respective processes at the site of their potential multiplication." → This gives students permission to borrow techniques across disciplines.🔴 Theory — Technique as passage: "A technique involves activating a passage between creative forces." It involves "practiced repetition and intensive exchange." Play and experimentation extend this.🟢 Pedagogic — Class as event: "For an 'event' to be an event, it is necessary that a collective thinking process be enacted that can give rise to new thoughts through the interaction on site. It is equally important that potential for what might occur not be pre-reduced to the delivery of already-arrived-at conclusions." → Approach seminar sessions this way.🔵 Project Hook — Co-causal thirdness: "Each of our events seeks collectively to find modalities of experimentation that connect practices at the levels of their intensive creative force. This is done not in order to map them onto one another, or to evaluate one in terms of another, but to propose a co-causal thirdness of exploration that can be generative of new modes of practice and inquiry." → The course as a whole is this kind of event. Manning & Massumi say research-creation happens "before research and creation diverge." What does that mean for how you currently describe your practice? Where do you typically put the boundary? What's the difference between framing a project and conditioning one? Think of a project you've done and ask: was it framed or conditioned? What enabling constraints are already active in your tools, materials, and methods — and which ones do you want to bring into play deliberately? "Unconstrained interaction rarely yields worthwhile effects." Do you agree? What's the minimum constraint needed for something interesting to happen? How does your institution (Drexel, your discipline) shape what "results" your work is supposed to produce? How can immanent critique operate from inside that? [Ch. 3, selected sections]
Assigned: Week 1, Week 2 🔴 Red = Core theoretical concept    🔵 Blue = Project / practice hook    🟢 Green = Pedagogic moment 🔴 Theory — Foundational claim (Hankins & Silverman): "Instruments have a life of their own. They do not merely follow theory; often they determine theory, because instruments determine what is possible, and what is possible determines to a large extent what can be thought." This is the core argument for the concept of epistemic tools — the tool is not neutral; it is an epistemic artifact, carrying a worldview into every act of use.🟢 Pedagogic — Course hardware rationale: Why do we use specific hardware in this course rather than staying entirely in software? Because the choice of instrument conditions what kinds of thinking and making are possible. The MPR121 capacitive touch sensor does not "just" detect touch — it frames touch as a particular kind of data. The Zoom H5 does not "just" record — it frames sound as a particular kind of capture.🔴 Theory — Three modalities of instrument relation (Ihde 1990): Embodiment relations: the instrument extends the body or amplifies the senses (we act through it) Hermeneutic relations: the instrument provides data we must interpret — like a spectrograph or heat map Alterity relations: the technology becomes something we engage with for its own sake — virtual reality, for instance, or a musical instrument that plays back 🔵 Project Hook — Entangled modalities: These relations are "not in isolation from one another, but are themselves an entangled web/knot." A single session working with TouchDesigner and a sensor involves all three simultaneously — you act through it (embodiment), read its outputs (hermeneutic), and sometimes play with it as its own thing (alterity). The task is to notice which mode is active and when.🔴 Theory — No neutral tool (Ihde 1979): "Technology equally conceals and reveals… Technologies organise, select, focus the task, and shape the environment through various transformations. This is what Ihde calls amplification-reduction transformations." Every tool amplifies certain features of the world and reduces others. There is no tool that is neutral.🔵 Project Hook — Inherited defaults as worldviews: Musical software carries embedded assumptions: "halftone equal tempered tuning, temporal quantisation, or note-based event model." These are not inevitable features of music — they are contingent historical choices now naturalized into default. → What defaults has your current software stack inherited? Which do you accept, which do you resist?🟢 Pedagogic — Tool critique is practice critique: "We must become critically aware of, navigate, and refute (become fugitives) when we pick and utilize certain tools. We must not subconsciously and unknowingly continue to present certain worldviews if they are not aligned with our being." This is not about avoiding tools — it is about practicing with a critical awareness of what they bring.🔴 Theory — Naturalization (Latour / Bowker & Star): "Objects establish themselves as black boxes through repeated use and in the process their origins disappear. The object is naturalised through heavy use, a fact prompting Bowker and Star to observe that the 'more naturalized the object becomes, the more unquestioning the relationship of the community to it; the more invisible the contingent and historical circumstances of its birth, the more it sinks into the community's routinely forgotten memory.'"🟢 Pedagogic — Black-boxing as danger: The danger is not complexity — it's forgetting. When we forget that a tool is a contingent artifact, we stop questioning it. CTP (Agre) and research-creation (Manning & Massumi) are both, in part, practices of deliberately opening black boxes back up.🔴 Theory — The separation and its questioning: "If the problem of Western philosophy has been the separation of techne and episteme, this dichotomy is now being questioned, following a better understanding in cognitive science and the role of active perception." The early modern conception: instruments are "containers of theory" — the musician engages with a system of thought when performing on an instrument.🔴 Theory — Three modes of epistemological work (Baird): Model knowledge: the instrument as material mode of representation Working knowledge: the instrument as mode of effective action Encapsulated knowledge: the instrument synthesizing representation and action together "Technological artefacts are models of thought, performing epistemological work alongside scientific theories, and often preceding them."🟢 Pedagogic — The historical question: When did instruments of the arts lose their epistemic status? When did the art instrument cease to be studied as a knowledge-making device? The interdisciplinary turn is, in part, a recovery of that status.🔴 Theory — Material / electric / symbolic: "The digital system is material in its body, electric in function, and symbolic in control." Unlike acoustic instruments, where most time with the instrument does not involve symbolic thought, digital instruments are fundamentally representational. "Behind our simple instrument are layers of microchips, busses, memory; operating systems, code libraries, classes; protocols, standards."🔵 Project Hook — Designer decides: "The designer decides what is revealed and what is concealed when the system is used." When the designer is also the performer, the researcher, and the observer — as in autoethnographic research practice — navigating these roles requires deliberate switching.🔵 Project Hook — Play as modality: "In music technologies, this manifests through play, through playing the instrument, but also the playful interaction that can emerge between a human and machine if the latter is given agency." The question of machine agency — explored in Somax2, in generative systems, in AI improvisation — is precisely the question of what kind of play becomes possible when the instrument pushes back. Pick one tool you use daily. What does it amplify about your practice? What does it reduce or make invisible? Magnusson says the digital system is "material in its body, electric in function, symbolic in control." What does the "symbolic" layer of your tool hide about the material layer underneath? Ihde describes embodiment, hermeneutic, and alterity relations with instruments. Which of these dominates your current hardware/software setup, and why? What in your current stack is a black box you've stopped questioning? What would happen if you opened it? Hankins & Silverman say tools determine theory. What theory is being determined by the specific hardware we're using in this course? Magnusson — Epistemic Tools

Primary readings due Week 03. Come having read both. One question or point of friction from each is enough. Chapter 3 (selected sections) Bloomsbury Academic, 2019.Access: Magnusson — Epistemic Tools PDFIn Bridging the Great Divide: Social Science, Technical Systems, and Cooperative Work. Lawrence Erlbaum, 1997.
Access: Agre — Critical Technical Practice PDFThese two texts work well together — Magnusson gives you the vocabulary for thinking about tools as epistemic artifacts, and Agre gives you the practice methodology for actually working inside that critique.For Magnusson: He's making a philosophical argument about instruments — that they are not neutral, that they determine what kinds of thinking are possible, and that every tool carries a worldview. Read it looking for the moments that describe your own tools. The amplification-reduction idea is the core — look for where he explains it and think immediately of a tool in your own stack.For Agre: This one is more personal — he's writing about his own attempt to reform AI from inside, and the difficulties he ran into. The concept of hassles is the most immediately practical thing in the text. A hassle is a recurring friction in a workflow that reveals a mismatch between how a tool models the world and how the world actually is. Hassles are data.Magnusson: Pick one tool you use regularly (hardware or software). What does it amplify about your practice? What does it reduce or make invisible? Magnusson says tools can become "black boxes" — things we stop questioning because they've been naturalized by use. What in your current stack have you stopped questioning? What would happen if you opened it back up? He describes three modes of relation to instruments: embodiment (you act through it), hermeneutic (you read its output), alterity (you play with it as its own thing). Which of these dominates how you use your primary tool — and does that shift depending on what you're doing? Agre: Identify one hassle in your current practice — a recurring friction, not a one-time frustration. What does it tell you about the assumptions built into the tool (or system, or workflow) causing it? Agre describes a "split identity" — one foot in craft, one foot in critique. What does that split feel like in your own work? Is there a tension between the two, or have you found a way to hold them together? You need to: Have read both texts at least once (a partial read beats a no-read) Have one concrete example ready — a tool, a hassle, or a moment where you felt a tool shaping what you could think Know which ideas land for you and which ones you're skeptical of — both are useful

digm-553/week-02-construct-conditions-fo.title: (Im)material Potluck
digm-553/week-02-construct-conditions-fo.description:
Each person brings one (im)material thing. We find out what it knows. This is the first collective event of the course. You brought something. I brought something. We're going to put them all in the same room and see what happens when we actually talk about them.Collective Practice
Enabling Constraints
Physical-Digital Entanglement
Research-CreationFor each contribution we're working through the same three questions:1. What does it resist? What does it yield to? Not what it is, but what it does. What happens when you push on it? 2. What does it already know? Every material, tool, or dataset carries embedded logic: assumptions about what it's for, what it can sense, what it makes legible. What worldview is already in the thing you brought? 3. What would it take to put this in a signal chain? What sensor, protocol, or system could turn its behavior into data? What gets amplified? What gets lost?I brought three things together…What it is: A portable audio recorder with interchangeable capsule system (XY stereo capsule default) + 2 additional inputs for external mics or line sources.What it resists: It's designed to capture sound above water, through air. The diaphragm is optimized for atmospheric pressure and airborne sound waves. Submerge it and it fails. That failure is a constraint. What it yields to: Everything in its polar pattern, within its frequency response curve. It's extraordinarily accurate and faithful. Which means it also captures everything you didn't intend (room noise, handling noise, etc.). That is another of its constraints.What it knows: That sound is something that moves through air, that has amplitude and frequency, that can be captured as a voltage signal. It doesn't know about pressure differentials in water, or the acoustic signature of dissolution, or what it means for a material to "sound like" something, culturally speaking. Signal chain position: Capture device → digital audio file → DAW or Max/MSP → granular synthesis or convolution. The H5 is the first transduction point.What it is: A piezoelectric contact microphone sealed in an epoxy housing — built to go into water. Where the H5 fails, this picks up at that moment. What it resists: Atmospheric sound (it's designed to be submerged). High-frequency detail in air is lost. It is more “optimized” for the acoustic properties of water, which transmit certain frequencies differently than air. It also resists damage from submersion that would destroy a conventional diaphragm mic.What it yields to: Pressure waves propagating through liquid (including the sounds that materials make as they dissolve, swell, crack, and settle). The crackle of a substrate fracturing under water. The CO₂ fizz of an effervescent reaction. What it knows: That sound can travel through a medium that isn't air. That water has its own acoustic logic. That a piezo element converts mechanical pressure directly to voltage.Signal chain position: Hydrophone → H5 mic input → digital audio → Max/RNBO granular patch. The hydrophone acts as the second transduction: physical pressure → electrical signal. What it is: A bath bomb-style compressed “sphere” (more like loose moon-sand right now) made from baking soda, citric acid, cornstarch, clay (bentonite or kaolin), salts, and iron oxide pigment. Designed to dissolve in water over 10–40 minutes, producing acoustic, visual, and chemical events as it does. What it resists: Dissolution is its enabling constraint and its generative condition. The sphere is structurally stable in dry conditions; contact with water is the co-cause that activates its temporal properties.What it yields to: Water. Heat. Time. Each material layer artifact or suspends at a different rate. The iron oxide creates ink-like plumes The bentonite swells before dispersing, clouding the water The salt crystals fracture and dissolve with audible cracks What it knows (by design): The sphere is built from materials chosen for both their cultural and sonic resonances (obsidian black, earth tones, water-soluble minerals). For this, chemistry becomes a form of argument-in-action. The dissolution profile is activates a score. Signal chain position: Sphere in water → hydrophone captures acoustic events → H5 records → granular synthesis in Max/RNBO maps dissolution data to sound. The sphere is another instrument and the water the performance space. What does a material know; and what becomes audible when we put it in a signal chain? The H5 is designed for air. The hydrophone is designed for water. The sphere is designed to dissolve. The enabling constraint of these instruments arises from their combination. The three co-causes that produce something none of them could alone.(Populated during class — each student's object, their three-question responses, and any signal chain thinking that emerged in the room.)A few artists whose potluck logic is worth knowing:Zimoun — sound sculptures using mechanical components Simple materials (cardboard, wire, motors) combined with simple constraints (one motion, one material, repeated) to produce emergent acoustic complexity. The constraint is reductive; the result is not.
→ zimoun.netChristine Sun Kim — sound as material / Game of Skill 2.0 Kim works with sound as a material to be shaped, exploring how sound carries social power, and what it means to control vs. be controlled by sonic space as a Deaf artist. The "constraint" of Deafness becomes the condition for new forms.
→ christinesunkim.com
→ https://rhizome.org/editorial/2015/oct/30/artist-profile-christine-sun-kim/
→ https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cJvys3curssMendi + Keith Obadike — Blackness for Sale (2001) / sonic practice An eBay listing offering his [Keith Obadike’s] "Blackness" for sale: the platform's auction logic is the constraint; the listing becomes a conceptual artwork about how Blackness is commodified and sold. The tool's assumptions are turned against themselves.
→ https://elmcip.net/creative-work/blackness-sale
→ https://direct.mit.edu/books/edited-volume/4374/chapter-abstract/187414/The-Black-Net-Art-Actions-Blackness-for-Sale-2001?redirectedFrom=fulltextTristan Perich — 1-Bit Symphony (2010) An entire symphony composed for a single-bit audio chip: 1 or 0, on or off, no in between. The computational constraint becomes the aesthetic. The limitation and the emergence is the timbre and msuic.
→ tristanperich.com
→ https://cantaloupemusic.com/albums/1-bit-symphony
→ https://arts.mit.edu/tristan-perichs-1-bit-symphony/
The potluck feeds directly into the workshop — W02B. You'll take what you just described and push it further: an effort to convert a limitative constraint to an enabling one, and (conceptually) put an object in the signal chain.
