digm-553/week-02-construct-conditions-fo.title: Enabling Constraints Workshop
digm-553/week-02-construct-conditions-fo.description:
A limitation that, through interaction with other forces, generates emergence rather than just restriction. The goal today is to do our best to feel and operate an enabling constraint. We're going to work with what we brought and see what happens when we push on its limits.Enabling Constraints
Research-Creation
Physical-Digital EntanglementFor Manning & Massumi: gravity is implacable. You can't dance without it. You can jump without it. There are many aspects of our daily lives and activates that would be impossible without it. Gravity thus, enables the possible. Now, take the jump. Add horizontal momentum and you get an arc: a collaboration between two co-causes. Neither gravity nor momentum alone makes the jump. The constraint is generative because of its resistance.The question this opens: What's the gravity in your object? What does it resist that you could push against? Place your object on the shared surface. Describe it — but you cannot use the words "material" or "art."Instead, try: What does it resist? What does it yield to? What does it amplify? What does it reduce? What can not be done with it? (That's your starting constraint.) What does it do to the thing closest to it? Pick one thing your object cannot do. One real limitation.Now: what second thing (a co-cause) could convert that limitation into generative potential?The co-cause can be: Another object or material A rule or instruction A body position or gesture A sensor or signal chain A time constraint Write down the pair: [limitation] + [co-cause] → [what becomes possible]You're designing an enabling constraint.Pick one object from the table. [Conceptually] connect your object to a sensor. (or if you have the stuff, you could actually do it)At the moment of connection: pause. Ask: What just happened to this object? What did it become? What does the sensor now "know" about the object? What doesn't it know? What's being amplified? What's being reduced? Write 2–3 sentences: what did the object become when it entered the signal chain?This is the physical-digital entanglement moment — a foreign object enters a circuit and both things change.Return to your original object. Describe it again — same no-"material"/no-"art" constraint from Round 1, but now you've been through the workshop.Did your description change? If yes: what changed it? If no: what does that tell you about how you're relating to this object?Group discussion: what's the enabling constraint of the workshop itself?A few works where the constraint is the piece, not an obstacle to it:Alvin Lucier — I Am Sitting in a Room (1969) The room's acoustic resonance is the constraint. Lucier records himself speaking, plays it back into the room, records that, plays it back again, until the room's frequencies overtake his voice entirely. The limitation (imperfect playback in a reverberant space) becomes the compositional process.
→ Listen / readNeri Oxman — Material Ecology / Silk Pavilion (2013) The constraint is the silkworm's biology: it can only spin within certain temperature and humidity ranges, following pheromone traces. Oxman designs the armature; the worms design the surface. The biological constraint shapes the architecture.

→ Deep Listening InstituteTorkwase Dyson — Black Compositional Thought (ongoing) Dyson uses the constraint of a fixed geometric vocabulary — arcs, rectangles, horizontal planes — to think spatial liberation for Black bodies. The limitation of the vocabulary becomes the condition for specificity.

See Readings for full citations.Week 11Spring 2026A map of the course's entanglements — weeks and their conceptual threads.BEGINENDMaking and thinking as the same act — not phases, not sequence, not illustration.The standard model: you research something, then you make something that shows what you found. Research-creation refuses that split. Manning & Massumi locate it at what they call the prebifurcation point — the moment before making and thinking get separated into different institutional categories with different evaluation criteria. At that point, making is thinking, and thinking is already a practice.The thing this rules out is the communication model — the idea that your creative work is "delivering" research results you already had. If the project knows its outcome before it starts, it's not research-creation. The work has to be genuinely open to something it couldn't have predicted.What that actually requires in practice: conditioning rather than framing. Framing means you set up a structure and the work fills it in. Conditioning means you bring things into contact — materials, tools, questions, bodies, sensors — and stay open to what emerges from their interaction. Neither you nor any individual element fully determines the outcome.For this course: the journal is not documentation of a separate making process. The making is not an illustration of the thinking. They interpenetrate, or it's not research-creation.
Week 1, Week 2, Week 3, Week 4, Week 5, Week 6, Week 7, Week 8, Week 9, Week 10, Week 11 Where in your workflow do making and thinking actually happen at the same time? Can you work from that moment deliberately? Is your project conditioned or framed? What are you holding open, and what are you predetermining? If your practice is already "thinking something" — what is it thinking right now? What in your institution (program, discipline, grading rubric) separates your thinking from your making? How do you work inside that without just reproducing it?
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act* — Propositions 0–3.
Loveless — *Haraway's Dog* — on curiosity as a research method; following a question rather than testing a hypothesis.
Epistemic Tools   Enabling Constraints   Entanglement   Failure as Method   Making PublicResearch-CreationTools are not neutral. Every instrument encodes a worldview — a set of propositions about what the world is, what can be known about it, and who that knowledge is for.Magnusson, drawing on Hankins & Silverman and Don Ihde, argues that instruments don't merely follow theory — they often determine it, because "instruments determine what is possible, and what is possible determines to a large extent what can be thought." An epistemic tool is any instrument understood this way: as a knowledge-making artifact with its own claims built in.Ihde identifies three modalities of how instruments mediate between body and world: embodiment relations (you act through the tool, which recedes), hermeneutic relations (the tool produces data you must interpret), and alterity relations (you engage with the tool as a quasi-other). These aren't fixed categories — any practice oscillates between them, and the shift matters.Every tool also performs an amplification-reduction: it amplifies certain features of the world and systematically reduces others. The danger isn't reduction itself — all tools must reduce. The danger is when the reduction becomes invisible, when it gets naturalized into what Latour calls a black box: an object whose internal contingency has disappeared through repeated use. Fluency closes black boxes. The critique foot of Agre's split identity keeps reopening them.
Week 1, Week 2, Week 3, Week 4, Week 5 What does your primary tool amplify — what becomes easy, visible, measurable? And what does it reduce — what disappears, gets rounded off, or can't be represented? Who designed the defaults in your software? What assumptions about bodies, practices, and contexts are baked into those choices? Which of Ihde's three modalities describes your relationship to your tool right now? When does it shift — and what triggers the shift? What's the most naturalized tool in your practice — the one you've stopped questioning? What would happen if you opened that black box?
Magnusson — *Epistemic Tools* — the source text for the concept; covers Ihde's modalities, amplification-reduction, and the techne/episteme distinction.
Agre — *Critical Technical Practice* — on computational imperialism, the split identity, and the practice of making the invisible assumptions of tools visible.
Research-Creation   Enabling Constraints   Entanglement   Physical-Digital Entanglement   Failure as MethodEpistemic ToolsA constraint that opens things up rather than just closing them down.Manning & Massumi's example: gravity. You can't dance without gravity — remove it and there's no jump, no landing, no arc. Gravity is implacable, but it's also what makes the jump possible. Add horizontal momentum and "the arc of the jump will be a collaboration between the action of gravity and the energy and angular momentum of the horizontal movement acting as co-causes." That's an enabling constraint in action — resistance that generates something rather than just blocking it.The key distinction is between limitative constraints (dead ends) and enabling ones (co-causes). A limitative constraint just says stop. An enabling constraint pushes back in a way that makes something happen that wouldn't otherwise. The trick is figuring out which you're dealing with — and sometimes, how to convert one into the other.This shows up everywhere in the course. The MPR121 has 12 channels — that's a constraint, but it's also the specific sculptural logic of the thing. OSC over UDP drops packets — that's a constraint, but it forces real-time compositional decisions you wouldn't otherwise have to make. The 3-hour session is a constraint; it's also what allows the kind of depth you can't get in 50 minutes.
Week 1, Week 2, Week 3, Week 4, Week 5, Week 8 What's the gravity in your practice — the resistance you can't remove? Is it enabling or just limitative? What would it take to convert it? What's the difference between a constraint someone handed you and one you designed yourself? When you hit a wall, is it a dead end or a co-cause waiting to be found? What if you designed your constraints before you designed the content?
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act* — Propositions 0–3.
Research-Creation   Epistemic Tools   Entanglement   Failure as Method   Physical-Digital EntanglementEnabling ConstraintsPractitioner, tool, and material do not interact as pre-formed, separate entities. They are mutually constituted through the practice itself. You don't bring a self to a tool — the self that acts is partly made by the act.Barad's posthumanist performativity replaces interaction (between pre-existing things) with intra-action (the process through which distinct agencies emerge). An apparatus — for Barad, any material-discursive arrangement that makes knowledge possible — doesn't just measure or represent phenomena; it participates in producing them. The researcher, the instrument, and the phenomenon are all co-constituted through the apparatus.For this course, that means: you are not a stable subject using a neutral tool to study an external object. You are entangled with your hardware, your software, your materials, and the site of your practice. These entanglements are not metaphors — they are structural features of how knowledge gets made. Documenting them honestly is part of what the Critical Technical Journal is for.Camus & Vinck extend this into digital materiality: the digital is not immaterial. It is made of matter — servers, cables, electricity, screen light. Every "digital" thing has a thickness, a weight, a set of dependencies. The click is a material event. The file is an inscription on physical media. Recognizing this thickness is how you stop treating your tools as transparent windows onto some other reality.
Week 3, Week 4, Week 5, Week 6, Week 7, Week 8, Week 9 What are you entangled with in your current project — not just using, but mutually constituted by? What would change about the project if that entanglement changed? Barad replaces "interaction" with "intra-action." What's the difference? Try to locate an intra-action — a moment where the boundaries between you, your tool, and your material were genuinely unclear. Where does the "digital" in your practice have material weight — consume power, require infrastructure, produce heat, leave traces? If your apparatus (the whole material-discursive arrangement of your practice) is not just measuring phenomena but helping produce them — what phenomena is yours producing?
Camus + Vinck — *Unfolding Digital Materiality* — on the thickness of digital objects; the materiality of inscription and infrastructure.
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act* — the concept of co-causality and conditioning is entanglement in practice.
Research-Creation   Epistemic Tools   Enabling Constraints   Physical-Digital Entanglement   Failure as MethodEntanglementFailure and impasse are not obstacles to the project. They are data about the project — revealing the formative conditions, hidden assumptions, and structural tensions that define what the work is actually doing.Agre's concept of the hassle is foundational here: not a one-time crash, but a recurring friction — something that keeps happening at the same point in your workflow, for reasons you can't quite name. Hassles are worth writing down. They are the system telling you something structural about the gap between how your tool models the world and how the world actually works.The move Agre names — and this course practices — is to treat impasse as an intellectual resource. When something fails repeatedly, don't just fix it and move on. Ask: what assumption was I making that this failure is disconfirming? What was I treating as settled that isn't? These are the questions the Critical Technical Journal is built to hold.Manning & Massumi's concept of immanent critique is also relevant here: failure, encountered from inside the practice, reveals the pressure points of the system. You can't see those pressure points from outside. You find them by building, hitting walls, and noticing where the resistance is structural rather than incidental.
Week 5, Week 6, Week 7, Week 8, Week 9 What's a recurring friction in your current workflow — not a one-off problem, but something that keeps coming back? What is that hassle about? What assumption does it keep bumping against? When you hit a dead end in a project, how do you usually respond? Do you route around it, sit with it, or abandon it? What would it look like to study it instead? What's the difference between a failure that tells you something and one that doesn't? How do you tell them apart in the moment? If you had to name your most productive creative failure — the one that most changed how you work — what would you call it? What intermediation term would Agre give it?
Agre — *Critical Technical Practice* — the source of the hassle concept and the method of treating recurring friction as intellectual data.
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act* — immanent critique as the practice of finding pressure points from inside the system.
Research-Creation   Epistemic Tools   Enabling Constraints   Entanglement   Collective PracticeFailure as MethodPhysical and digital aren't two separate domains with an interface between them. They're entangled — each one shaping the other.The signal chain at the center of this course — body → sensor → microcontroller → protocol → software → output — is not a pipeline that converts physical reality into digital representation. It's a series of transformations. At each arrow, something is amplified and something is reduced. The body that touches a capacitive sensor is not the same as the threshold-crossing event the sensor registers. The OSC message is not the gesture. Something is always gained; something is always lost. The question is whether you know which — and whether that choice is deliberate.Magnusson puts it directly: the digital system is "material in its body, electric in function, and symbolic in control." All three layers are active at once. The hardware has physical affordances that shape where you can put it and what it can touch. The firmware has timing properties that shape resolution and latency. The software has representational assumptions that shape what the data means. None of these layers is neutral; together they constitute the instrument.This thread tracks how physical and digital forces meet, condition each other, and produce something neither could alone — across hardware choices, material selections, installation environments, and bodies moving through space.
Week 1, Week 2, Week 3, Week 4, Week 5, Week 6, Week 7, Week 8, Week 9, Week 10 At each arrow in your signal chain, what's being amplified and what's being reduced? Is that tradeoff intentional? What does your system not know about the body it's sensing — and what can happen in that gap? Where does the physical environment shape the digital behavior, and vice versa? Can you design the entanglement rather than just inheriting it? What material are your sensors touching? What cultural or social charge does that material carry — and does your system acknowledge it?
Magnusson — *Epistemic Tools* — on instruments as material-electric-symbolic systems.
Camus + Vinck — *Unfolding Digital Materiality* — on the thickness and materiality of digital objects.
Research-Creation   Epistemic Tools   Enabling Constraints   EntanglementPhysical-Digital EntanglementRendering work public is not the delivery of results. It is a continuation of the research — a way of making the formative conditions and processual transformation of the work available for encounter.Loveless, working through Haraway, argues that research-creation carries an obligation to render research public — not as a finished product submitted to evaluation, but as a practice in itself. What gets made public is not just the artifact but the forces that formed it: the impasses, the enabling constraints, the entanglements, the tools and their reductions. This is why the Final Presentation in this course is not a showcase. It is a rendering.The distinction Loveless makes is between transparency (showing your work) and accountability (taking responsibility for what your work does in the world — including what it can't do, what it excludes, and who it speaks to or past). Accountability requires knowing the stakes of the work, not just the process.For experimental media practice, making public also means confronting the question of audience: who is this for? What does it ask of the people who encounter it? A TouchDesigner patch sent to a hard drive is not public; the same patch running in a gallery space with bodies moving through it is. The difference is not technical. It is relational — and designing that relation is itself a creative and ethical act.
Week 6, Week 9, Week 11 What would it mean to make your process public — not just your result? What would you have to show that you've been hiding? Who is the audience for your work, and what does it ask of them? Have you designed that ask, or inherited it from the format? Loveless distinguishes transparency from accountability. Where in your practice are you being transparent (showing your method) without being accountable (owning what the work does or fails to do)? What form is your work made public in, and what does that form assume about who can access it?
Loveless — *Haraway's Dog* — on the obligation to render research public, curiosity as method, and the boundary object.
Research-Creation   Collective Practice   Failure as Method   EntanglementMaking PublicThe studio is not a bunch of individual practices running in parallel. It's a site where practitioners condition each other.Manning & Massumi describe the seminar or studio as an experiment: "For an 'event' to be an event, it is necessary that a collective thinking process be enacted that can give rise to new thoughts through the interaction on site." The key condition: what happens can't be predetermined. If the instructor already knows what conclusions are going to be reached and is just delivering them — that's not an event in this sense.The critique is the most direct version of this. In this course, critique is not judgment. It's activation — attending to someone else's work closely enough to surface what it's doing that it might not know it's doing. A good critique question doesn't say "this works / this doesn't." It opens something: what is this committed to? What does it refuse? What would happen if you followed that refusal further?There's an ethic here too. What you bring to the room — your presence, attention, honest response — is a contribution to a shared environment, not optional. This is part of how the work actually gets made.
Week 2, Week 6, Week 7, Week 8, Week 9, Week 11 What's the difference between a critique that evaluates and one that activates? What does an activating question actually sound like? What do you bring to the room that no one else does? What does the group gain from your specific presence? When you encounter someone else's work, what's your first instinct — assess it, identify with it, question it? What would it mean to just attend to it first? How does your practice change when it's in dialogue? What has a peer's question ever revealed to you about your own work?
Manning + Massumi — *Thought in the Act* — on the studio event and techniques of relation.
